task_title: Passengers, Seat Belts and Persons on Board
objective: By the end of this lesson you can state your Part 91 duties to passengers on belts, harnesses, seats, devices, crewmember interference and dropping objects, and give a complete passenger briefing for any flight.
why: The PIC must make sure every person on board is briefed on the belts and told to fasten them before the airplane moves. A tight belt is what lets a person survive a hard landing, and a quiet, briefed passenger is a help instead of a distraction. Safety belts, crewmembers at stations, careless operation and dropping objects are all on the AC 61-98E flight review checklist.

warmup: Think first: you are taking three friends for a flight. One has never flown in a small airplane, one brings an 18-month-old, and one wants to film the takeoff on a phone. What does the regulation make you tell them before you start the engine, and what else would you add?

key_terms.def: The person with final authority and responsibility for the operation and safety of the flight. The PIC must make sure passengers are briefed and belted.
A person assigned to perform duty in an aircraft during flight time. You, as the pilot, are one.
A pilot the aircraft or the operation requires. 91.105 says where they sit and when their belt and harness must be fastened.
The place each person must sit, with the safety belt and, if installed, shoulder harness fastened, during surface movement, takeoff and landing.
A child seat that may be used on board if it carries the right labels, is secured to a forward-facing seat, and the child is within its weight limit.
A harness and lanyard, not installed by FAA approval, that keeps a person inside the aircraft on doors-open or doors-off flights.
A carried-on electronic device such as a phone, tablet or laptop. 91.21 limits their use on some aircraft.
A medical portable electronic device that supports body functions. AC 91.21-1D says passengers may use them at all times.
A period with no talk or activity that is not needed for the flight. Required for airline and charter crews, recommended for everyone.
In 135.100: taxi, takeoff, landing, and all flight below 10,000 ft except cruise.
The PHAK memory aid for briefing passengers: Seat belts, Air vents, Fire extinguisher, Exit doors, Traffic and Talking, Your questions.
Operating an aircraft in a way that endangers the life or property of another. Banned by 91.13.

body.p: 91.107 puts two jobs on the pilot in command before the airplane moves. Both apply to a U.S.-registered civil aircraft, with only free balloons with a basket and some old airships left out [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(1)]].

callout.text: 91.107(a)(1): no pilot may take off unless the PIC ensures that each person on board is briefed on how to fasten and unfasten their safety belt and, if installed, shoulder harness [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(1)]].

91.107(a)(2): no pilot may move the aircraft on the surface, take off or land unless the PIC ensures each person on board has been notified to fasten their safety belt and, if installed, shoulder harness [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(2)]].

bullets: Briefing is about how the belt works. Notifying is the call to fasten it. You need both, and the notice comes before taxi, takeoff and landing [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(1)]] [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(2)]].

The rule says the PIC "ensures" it. Another person may say the words, but the duty stays with you. The PIC is directly responsible for, and the final authority as to, the operation of the aircraft [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3]].

The rule gives no exception for passengers who are pilots or who have flown with you before. The large airplane rule in 91.519 has a skip for familiar passengers; 91.107 does not [[60:534|14 CFR 91.519]] [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(1)]].

body.p: The FAA says GA pilots should always brief passengers before a flight. The briefing should hold your instructions for keeping distractions down and all the elements of 91.107(a)(1) and (2) [[15:17|AC 61-98E 2-9]]. Planning the briefing starts in the planning stage of the flight [[15:17|AC 61-98E 2-9]].

callout.text: Large airplanes and turbojet-powered multiengine airplanes fall under subpart F [[60:527|14 CFR 91.501]]. There, 91.519 requires an oral briefing on smoking, belts, doors and emergency exits, survival equipment, ditching and oxygen [[60:534|14 CFR 91.519]]. It does not apply to your piston single, but it is a good model for a full briefing.

check.q: What two things does 91.107(a) make the PIC ensure, and when?
check.a: That each person is briefed on how to fasten and unfasten the belt and harness before takeoff, and notified to fasten them before moving on the surface, takeoff and landing [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(1)]] [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(2)]].

chunks.title: Who must be belted, and when

callout.text: 91.107(a)(3): each person on board must occupy an approved seat or berth with a safety belt and, if installed, shoulder harness properly secured about them during movement on the surface, takeoff and landing [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)]].

head: Who
Belt
Shoulder harness
rows: Passengers
Surface movement, takeoff, landing [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)]]
Same times, if installed [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)]]
Required flight crewmembers
Fastened while at the station during takeoff, landing and en route [[60:441|14 CFR 91.105]]
Takeoff and landing, unless none is installed or you could not do your duties with it fastened [[60:441|14 CFR 91.105]]

body.p: 91.105 also keeps each required flight crewmember at their station during takeoff, landing and en route. You may leave only for duties connected with the flight or for physiological needs [[60:441|14 CFR 91.105]]. People covered by 91.105 are not covered by 91.107(a)(3) [[60:442|14 CFR 91.107(b)]]. 91.107 also does not apply to operations under part 121, 125 or 135 unless stated [[60:442|14 CFR 91.107(b)]].

callout.text: Note: the PHAK SAFETY list says shoulder harness fastened for takeoff and landing [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]]. 91.107(a)(3) also covers an installed harness during movement on the surface [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)]]. The CFR is the rule, so brief belts and harnesses on for taxi too.

body.p: The rule says nothing about passenger belts in cruise. Turbulence can still throw people around. In moderate turbulence occupants feel definite strains against belts and loose objects are dislodged. In severe turbulence occupants are forced violently against their belts and loose objects are tossed about [[34:106|AIM TBL 7-1-11]].

Check the restraints on every preflight. Belts and harnesses should be free from fraying, latch properly and be securely attached. Seats should latch into the rails through the lock pins, and the rail holes should not be worn oval [[24:41|AFH 2-4]].

check.q: During taxi, does a passenger in a seat with an installed shoulder harness have to wear it?
check.a: Yes. 91.107(a)(3) covers the belt and, if installed, the harness during movement on the surface, takeoff and landing [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)]].

chunks.title: Children, sport parachutists and doors-off flights

body.p: 91.107(a)(3) lists three ways a person may be on board without their own belted seat [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)]].

head: Case
What the rule allows
Limits
rows: Lap child
Held by an adult who is in an approved seat or berth [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)(i)]]

Child has not reached the second birthday and does not occupy or use any restraining device [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)(i)]]. Not allowed with doors open or removed, or when the adult uses a supplemental restraint system [[60:445|14 CFR 91.108(j)]]
Sport parachutist
May use the floor as a seat [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)(ii)]]
Only when on board for sport parachuting [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)(ii)]]
Child in a child seat
May use an approved child restraint system [[60:442|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)(iii)]]

Child is with a parent, guardian or attendant the parent or guardian designated. Seat properly secured to an approved forward-facing seat or berth, child properly secured and not over the seat's weight limit, seat bears the right labels [[60:442|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)(iii)]]

bullets: U.S.-standard seats made January 1, 1981 to February 25, 1985: one label saying the seat conforms to all applicable Federal motor vehicle safety standards [[60:442|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)(iii)]].

U.S.-standard seats made on or after February 26, 1985: two labels, that same statement plus "THIS RESTRAINT IS CERTIFIED FOR USE IN MOTOR VEHICLES AND AIRCRAFT" in red lettering [[60:442|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)(iii)]].

Any other seat: a label or markings showing it was made under United Nations standards, or that the FAA approved it (by type certificate or STC, under 21.8(d), or under TSO-C100b or a later version) [[60:442|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)(iii)]].
Booster seats, vest and harness types, and lap-held child restraints are not approved for use in aircraft, unless FAA-approved in one of those ways [[60:442|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)(iii)]].

callout.text: Watch out: a baby carrier or vest worn by a parent is a restraining device. A lap child must not use any restraining device [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)(i)]], and vest and harness types are not approved [[60:442|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)(iii)]].

body.p: Doors-off or doors-open flights, such as photo flights, have their own rule. Each person stays in a belted approved seat the whole flight, or is belted for surface movement, takeoff and landing and wears a supplemental restraint system the rest of the time [[60:443|14 CFR 91.108(a)-(b)]]. Each such passenger must be briefed on how to use and release it and how you will talk to them, then show they can work the belt and the quick release before ground movement [[60:445|14 CFR 91.108(g)-(h)]]. No one under 15, no one seated in the flight deck and no one in a child seat may use one [[60:445|14 CFR 91.108(i)]].

callout.text: Changed: the only source note under 91.108 is Docket FAA-2023-2250, Amdt. 91-376, 89 FR 67849, Aug. 22, 2024, so the section is new with that amendment [[60:446|14 CFR 91.108]]. The 91.107 amendment list ends with the same docket [[60:443|14 CFR 91.107]].

check.q: A mother wants to hold her 20-month-old in a front-pack carrier strapped to her chest. Allowed?
check.a: No. A child under 2 may be held only if the child does not occupy or use any restraining device [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)(i)]].

chunks.title: Why belts matter: the physics of a crash landing

body.p: The AFH says avoiding crash injuries is largely a matter of keeping the cabin intact and avoiding forceful contact with the inside of the cabin. The second part is a matter of seat and body security [[24:351|AFH 18-2]].

callout.text: An intact cabin helps only if the person slows down with it. A loose occupant is stopped violently in a "secondary collision" [[24:351|AFH 18-2]].

bullets: Groundspeed matters most. Doubling it quadruples the destructive energy [[24:352|AFH 18-3]].
Light airplanes are designed to protect occupants in crash landings of 9G forward [[24:352|AFH 18-3]].
At a uniform 9G, stopping from 50 mph takes about 9.4 ft. From 100 mph it takes about 37.6 ft, four times as far [[24:352|AFH 18-3]].

body.p: Application: a seat that slides on worn rails, or a harness left loose, lets the body move before the belt takes the load. That is why the preflight seat and belt check [[24:41|AFH 2-4]] and a snug belt for every landing belong in the briefing.

check.q: Per the AFH, what happens to destructive energy if touchdown groundspeed doubles?

chunks.title: Careless or reckless, interference and dropping objects

head: Rule
What it says
Who it binds
rows: No person may assault, threaten, intimidate or interfere with a crewmember doing their duties aboard an aircraft being operated [[60:436|14 CFR 91.11]]
Every person on board, passengers included
No person may operate an aircraft in a careless or reckless manner so as to endanger the life or property of another [[60:436|14 CFR 91.13]]
Anyone operating the aircraft
Same ban for operations other than air navigation, on the parts of an airport used by aircraft for air commerce [[60:436|14 CFR 91.13]]
Anyone operating on those airport surfaces
No PIC may allow an object to be dropped in flight that creates a hazard to persons or property [[60:437|14 CFR 91.15]]
The PIC

body.p: A crewmember is a person assigned to perform duty in an aircraft during flight time [[60:4|14 CFR 1.1]]. Flight time starts when the aircraft moves under its own power for the purpose of flight [[60:7|14 CFR 1.1]]. 91.11 itself says only "aboard an aircraft being operated" [[60:436|14 CFR 91.11]]. Interpretation: reading the definitions together, you are a crewmember once you taxi for flight; the rule text does not say more.

callout.text: 91.15 is not a total ban. It does not prohibit dropping any object if reasonable precautions are taken to avoid injury or damage to persons or property [[60:437|14 CFR 91.15]].

bullets: Part 135 has the same interference wording in 135.120 [[6:37|14 CFR 135.120]].

Interpretation: what counts as "careless," "reckless" or "reasonable precautions" is not defined in 91.13 or 91.15 [[60:436|14 CFR 91.13]] [[60:437|14 CFR 91.15]]. The FAA decides case by case, and those decisions are not in our sources.
Loose items are a dropping and a control risk. Before entering turbulence the AIM says tighten your belt, put on the shoulder harness and secure all loose objects [[34:120|AIM 7-1-27b1]].

callout.text: Brief the "hands off" rule. Application: tell passengers which controls not to touch and how you will ask for help. The PHAK suggests telling passengers about the controls and what they do [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]].

check.q: A passenger wants to toss a small sandbag out over an empty field to see it hit. What decides whether 91.15 allows it?
check.a: Whether the object creates a hazard to persons or property, and whether reasonable precautions are taken to avoid injury or damage [[60:437|14 CFR 91.15]]. It is the PIC's call and the PIC's responsibility.

callout.text: 91.21(a): no person may operate, and no operator or PIC may allow the operation of, any PED on a U.S.-registered civil aircraft operated by an air carrier or operating certificate holder, or on any other aircraft while it is operated under IFR [[60:438|14 CFR 91.21(a)]].

head: Excepted from 91.21(a)
Source
rows: Portable voice recorders, hearing aids, heart pacemakers, electric shavers
Any other PED the operator has determined will not interfere with the aircraft's navigation or communication system
Who decides: the certificate holder for its aircraft; for other aircraft, the PIC or other operator

body.p: So on a VFR flight in a non-certificated operation, 91.21(a) does not apply [[60:438|14 CFR 91.21(a)]]. Under IFR in your own airplane, you are the one who decides which devices are fine [[60:438|14 CFR 91.21(c)]]. AC 91.21-1D uses "operator" to mean the PIC, renter-pilot or certificate holder [[43:2|AC 91.21-1D 6.1]], and says only the operator is responsible for permitting a PED technology [[43:4|AC 91.21-1D 7.1]].

bullets: If the aircraft has not been shown PED tolerant, the operator may allow PED use during cruise. If a PED causes interference, isolate it, note the conditions, and turn it off [[43:5|AC 91.21-1D 7.2.3]].

Cell phones: the FCC prohibits airborne cellular telephone operation (47 CFR 22.925). The FAA allows phones on the ground. Airborne, passengers should turn phones off, disable cellular transmit, or use airplane mode [[43:7|AC 91.21-1D 9.1]] [[43:7|AC 91.21-1D 9.2]].

Medical devices that support body functions may be used at all times and need not be switched off. Small ones should be secured on the person during surface movement, takeoff, descent, approach and landing [[43:9|AC 91.21-1D 11]].
Your tablet is a PED too. Any PED use must be evaluated by the user or operator before use so it will not interfere with the aircraft [[42:2|AC 91-78A 7.2]].

body.p: AC 91.21-1D also says to tell passengers your device rules in the departure briefing or other ways, and to cover when devices must be stowed and what to do about a device fire or smoke [[43:5|AC 91.21-1D 8.1]] [[43:5|AC 91.21-1D 8.2]].

check.q: Which four devices does 91.21(b) except by name?
check.a: Portable voice recorders, hearing aids, heart pacemakers and electric shavers [[60:438|14 CFR 91.21(b)]].

body.p: No Part 91 rule requires a sterile flight deck. The rule is in part 121 (121.542) and part 135 (135.100) [[29:22|IPH 1-6]] [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. The AIH says that while it grew out of airline accidents, it holds true for the entire aviation community [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

head: Source
When to keep quiet
rows: PHAK
From departure to the first intermediate altitude and clearance from the local airspace, and on arrival from the first radar vector or descent for the approach [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]]
From when preflight preparations begin until clear of the terminal area and at cruising altitude, and from when landing preparations begin until stopped at the terminal [[7:5|AC 91-73B 7c]]
During critical phases such as taxi, takeoff and landing, with no extraneous talk or cell phone use [[15:17|AC 61-98E 2-9]]
Critical phases: all ground operations involving taxi, takeoff and landing, and all flight below 10,000 ft except cruise [[6:33|14 CFR 135.100]]

bullets: In PHAK Figure 2-20, task requirements rise at takeoff and peak during approach and landing [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]]. That is where a chatty passenger costs the most.
Phones and devices are discouraged during taxi, and everyone on board should turn them off then [[7:5|AC 91-73B 7b(j)]].
Remind occupants about the sterile cockpit, but encourage them to speak up if they see a conflict [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b]].
Distraction with passengers and focus on tablets reduce how often you scan for traffic [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15g1(a)]].

callout.text: Turn the passenger into a resource. The right-seat passenger should help scan for traffic [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15c]], may hold the chart [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]], or can read a checklist [[30:46|RMH 6-3]]. Keep them informed when the workload is low [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]].

check.q: Is a sterile flight deck required by Part 91 for your personal flight?
check.a: No. It is required for part 121 and 135 crews [[29:22|IPH 1-6]] [[6:33|14 CFR 135.100]], and the FAA recommends it for everyone [[25:179|AIH 9-9]] [[15:17|AC 61-98E 2-9]].

chunks.title: Risk: skipping or rushing the briefing

body.p: An unbriefed passenger does not know how to get out, how to help, or when to stay quiet. The RMH sample flight risk tool scores "Do you brief your passengers on the ground and in flight?" as 0 for yes and 2 for no [[30:28|RMH 3-10]].

head: Item not briefed
What can go wrong
Source
rows: Belts and harness
A loose occupant takes a secondary collision in a crash landing
Doors and exits
A door that opens in flight pulls attention from flying. Do not unbuckle to reach it. Land as soon as practicable and close it on the ground
Fire extinguisher and air vents
Use the extinguisher first, then open the vents to clear smoke; close them if the smoke gets worse
ELT
Pilots and passengers should know how to activate it manually and check it is transmitting
Parachute or Emergency Autoland, if installed
Parachute: brief passengers who can reach the handle on when it would be used and the basic steps. Autoland: a passenger can activate it manually
Talking
Distraction in high workload phases

callout.text: Watch out: aircraft differ. LSA doors and canopies can latch very differently, and a canopy that pops open can become an emergency in seconds. Practice the latches yourself first [[24:346|AFH 17-12]].

body.p: Seaplane flights add life vests. Writing about seaplanes, the AIM calls it imperative to brief passengers on the location and proper use of the flotation gear before leaving the dock [[34:166|AIM 7-6-9e]].

check.q: On the RMH sample FRAT, how many points does "no" to briefing passengers add?

chunks.title: Fly it step by step: a complete passenger briefing

body.p: **Build it from the rule, then add the SAFETY list.** The legal core is 91.107(a)(1) and (a)(2) [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(1)]] [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(2)]]. The PHAK SAFETY list fills in the rest [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]].

bullets: 1. Preflight: check belts, harnesses and seat locks [[24:41|AFH 2-4]].
2. At the airplane, before engine start: show each person how to fasten and unfasten the belt and harness, and have them do it [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(1)]].
3. Seat adjusted and locked; air vents and what to do if they feel unwell; fire extinguisher; doors, exits and the evacuation plan; survival kit [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]].
4. Traffic: how to point out other aircraft. Talking: when you need quiet, and that they should still speak up about a conflict [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]] [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b]].
5. Devices: phones to airplane mode and stowed for taxi, takeoff and landing; any device limits for this flight [[43:7|AC 91.21-1D 9.2]] [[7:5|AC 91-73B 7b(j)]].

6. Add-ons: route, altitude, time en route, weather, controls and what they do, smoking, and the airplane's limits [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]]. ELT and, if installed, parachute or autoland [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4a2(f)]] [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].
7. "Your questions?" [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]].
8. Before taxi, and again before takeoff and landing: "Belts and harnesses fastened?" [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(2)]].

callout.text: Application, a sample close: "From now until we level off, and again from when we start down until we park, please hold questions unless you see another airplane or something wrong. Then speak up right away." This matches the AC 91-73B and PHAK windows [[7:5|AC 91-73B 7c]] [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]].

At a flight review, AC 61-98E lists Safety Belts (91.107), Flightcrew Members at Station (91.105), Careless or Reckless Operation (91.13) and Dropping Objects (91.15) [[15:40|AC 61-98E App E]]. Be ready to give the briefing out loud.

check.q: Which steps of this briefing are required by regulation for your piston single, and which are guidance?
check.a: Required: briefing how to fasten and unfasten the belt and harness, and notifying everyone to fasten them before taxi, takeoff and landing [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(1)]] [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(2)]]. The rest is FAA guidance [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]] [[15:17|AC 61-98E 2-9]].

head: Error
Fix
rows: Briefing only "buckle up" without showing how the belt opens
Brief how to fasten and unfasten [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(1)]]
Passengers taking the shoulder harness off for taxi
Passengers wear an installed harness during surface movement too [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)]]
Lap child in a carrier, vest or booster
No restraining device for a lap child; boosters and vests not approved [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)(i)]] [[60:442|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)(iii)]]
Thinking the FAA bans all phones on every flight
91.21 covers certificate holders and IFR; the airborne cell ban is the FCC's [[60:438|14 CFR 91.21(a)]] [[43:7|AC 91.21-1D 9.1]]
Assuming any drop is illegal, or any drop is fine
Legal only if it creates no hazard, with reasonable precautions [[60:437|14 CFR 91.15]]
Chatting through taxi and the approach
Set the sterile periods in the briefing [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]] [[7:5|AC 91-73B 7c]]
Unbuckling to close a door that popped open
Fly the airplane, leave the door, land when practicable [[24:366|AFH 18-17]]

check.q: Your passenger is a pilot friend. Can you skip the 91.107(a)(1) briefing?
check.a: No. It covers each person on board and has no exception for experience [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(1)]].

scenario.title: Four seats, one door, IFR to the lake
scenario.setup: You are flying a Piper PA-28-181 (four seats, one door on the right side) with three adults to a lake airport. A marine layer means you have filed IFR. Your right-seat passenger has never flown in a small airplane and is nervous. One rear passenger plans to work on a laptop. The other is a pilot friend who says, "Skip the briefing, I know Pipers."

questions.q: What must you brief and notify by regulation, and does your pilot friend get a pass?
questions.a: Each person must be briefed on how to fasten and unfasten the belt and harness, and notified to fasten them before taxi, takeoff and landing [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(1)]] [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(2)]]. The rule has no experience exception.

questions.q: Why spend extra time on the door in this airplane?
questions.a: There is one door, and the right-seat passenger sits next to it. The SAFETY list covers how to secure and open exit doors and the evacuation plan [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]]. If it pops open in flight, no one unbuckles to reach it; you fly a normal pattern and land [[24:366|AFH 18-17]].

questions.q: May the rear passenger run the laptop on this IFR flight?
questions.a: Only if you, as PIC, determine it will not interfere with the navigation or communication systems [[60:438|14 CFR 91.21(a)]] [[60:438|14 CFR 91.21(b)]] [[60:438|14 CFR 91.21(c)]]. If you see interference, have it turned off [[43:5|AC 91.21-1D 7.2.3]].

questions.q: When do you ask for quiet, and what do you still want to hear?
questions.a: From when preflight preparations begin until clear of the terminal area and at cruising altitude, and from the start of landing preparations until stopped [[7:5|AC 91-73B 7c]] (the PHAK window is similar [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]]). They should still speak up if they see a conflict [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b]].

questions.q: In smooth cruise a rear passenger wants to unbuckle to reach a bag. Legal? What do you say?
questions.a: 91.107(a)(3) requires belts for surface movement, takeoff and landing [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)]], so it is not illegal. Application: ask them to stay belted anyway, since moderate turbulence brings definite strain against belts and dislodges loose objects [[34:106|AIM TBL 7-1-11]].

questions.q: On the approach the nervous passenger grabs the yoke. What rule covers it, and how should the briefing have prevented it?
questions.a: No person may interfere with a crewmember in the performance of duties [[60:436|14 CFR 91.11]], and you are the final authority on the operation [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3]]. The briefing should cover controls and what they do [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]]; application: say plainly "hands off the controls."

skills.do: Given an airplane, a flight and a group of passengers (including a child, a device user or a nervous first-timer), give a complete briefing out loud: how to fasten and unfasten belts and harnesses, when they must be fastened, seats, vents, extinguisher, doors and exits, traffic, sterile periods, devices and questions. Then say which parts 91.107 requires and which are guidance.
skills.practice: Write your own one-page briefing card for the airplane you fly, built on 91.107(a)(1) and (a)(2) [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(1)]] and the SAFETY list [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]]. Add the sterile windows [[7:5|AC 91-73B 7c]] and your device rules [[43:7|AC 91.21-1D 9.2]]. Read it to a friend at the airplane and time it, then give it at your next flight review, where AC 61-98E lists 91.107 [[15:40|AC 61-98E App E]].

options: Location of the fire extinguisher and survival kit
How to fasten and unfasten the safety belt and, if installed, shoulder harness
Where the emergency exits are and how to open them
When smoking is prohibited
quiz.why: The PIC must ensure each person is briefed on how to fasten and unfasten the belt and, if installed, harness [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(1)]]. The other items are good practice [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]] or are in the large airplane rule [[60:534|14 CFR 91.519]].

quiz.q: Under 91.107(a)(3), who may use the floor of the aircraft as a seat?
options: A crewmember on a ferry flight
A person on board for sport parachuting
A child under 2
Any passenger when all seats are full
quiz.why: A person on board to engage in sport parachuting may use the floor as a seat [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)(ii)]].

quiz.q: Under 91.105, when must a required flight crewmember's shoulder harness be fastened?
options: At all times in flight
During takeoff and landing, unless none is installed or it prevents required duties
Only during IFR approaches
Only when passengers are on board
quiz.why: During takeoff and landing, with exceptions when no harness is installed or duties cannot be done with it fastened [[60:441|14 CFR 91.105]].

quiz.q: A lap child under 2 may be held by an adult if:
options: The child wears an approved harness vest
The adult is in an approved seat or berth and the child uses no restraining device
The flight is VFR and under 1 hour
The pilot holds a commercial certificate
quiz.why: The adult must occupy an approved seat or berth, and the child must not occupy or use any restraining device [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)(i)]].

quiz.q: What does 91.15 say about dropping objects in flight?
options: It is always prohibited
It needs prior ATC approval
It is not prohibited if reasonable precautions are taken to avoid injury or damage
It is allowed only over open water
quiz.why: The PIC may not allow a drop that creates a hazard, but the section does not prohibit dropping objects with reasonable precautions [[60:437|14 CFR 91.15]].

quiz.q: 91.21(a) restricts PED use on which aircraft?
options: All U.S.-registered aircraft at all times
Aircraft of air carrier or operating certificate holders, and any other aircraft under IFR
Only aircraft above 10,000 ft
Only aircraft with glass cockpits
quiz.why: Those are the two groups in 91.21(a) [[60:438|14 CFR 91.21(a)]].

quiz.q: Under 91.21, who may decide a passenger's tablet will not interfere, in an airplane that is not operated by a certificate holder?
options: Only the FAA
The device maker
The pilot in command or other operator
The passenger
quiz.why: For aircraft other than certificate holders', the determination may be made by the PIC or other operator [[60:438|14 CFR 91.21(c)]].

quiz.q: Per the PHAK, a sterile flight deck on departure lasts from departure until:
options: The first intermediate altitude and clearance from the local airspace
Reaching 10,000 ft MSL
The top of the traffic pattern
Contact with approach control
quiz.why: From departure to the first intermediate altitude and clearance from the local airspace [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]].

quiz.q: Smoke fills the cabin from a suspected electrical fire. Per the AFH, when should the cabin air vents be opened?
options: Immediately, before anything else
After the fire extinguisher (if available) is used; close them if the smoke gets worse
Never in flight
Only after landing
quiz.why: Use the extinguisher first, then open the vents to purge smoke; if smoke increases, close them at once [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]. This is why the briefing covers the extinguisher and the vents [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]].

final_quiz.q: During taxi your back-seat passenger slips off the shoulder harness to reach a bag, saying harnesses are only for takeoff and landing. What applies?
options: Fine: the PHAK lists harnesses for takeoff and landing only
Not allowed: an installed harness must be secured during movement on the surface too
Fine, as long as the lap belt stays on and you taxi slowly
Not allowed only at towered airports
final_quiz.why: 91.107(a)(3) covers the belt and, if installed, harness during movement on the surface, takeoff and landing [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)]]. The PHAK SAFETY line lists the harness for takeoff and landing [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]]; the CFR is the rule.

final_quiz.q: A family brings a 3-year-old and a booster seat labeled only for motor vehicles. What is the legal setup?
options: Lap child on a parent
Booster seat on the rear bench
Own approved seat with belt, or an approved, labeled child restraint system on a forward-facing seat
Parent holds the child with the parent's belt around both
final_quiz.why: Only a child who has not reached the second birthday may be held [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)(i)]]. Boosters are not approved; an approved seat needs the right labels on a forward-facing seat [[60:442|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)(iii)]].

final_quiz.q: A doors-off photo flight. A passenger wants to hold her 1-year-old. What does Part 91 say?
options: Allowed if both wear supplemental restraints
Allowed if the child is under 2
Not allowed: no lap child when the doors are opened or removed
Allowed below 1,000 ft AGL only
final_quiz.why: A child under 2 may not be held when the aircraft doors are opened or removed [[60:445|14 CFR 91.108(j)]].

final_quiz.q: You are VFR in your club's airplane. A passenger wants to run a tablet game during cruise. Which is correct?
options: 91.21(a) prohibits it
91.21(a) does not apply on this flight; you still judge whether it is a distraction and watch for interference
Allowed only in airplane mode under 91.21(b)
Allowed only with an EFB authorization
final_quiz.why: 91.21(a) covers certificate holders' aircraft and other aircraft under IFR [[60:438|14 CFR 91.21(a)]]. Any PED should be evaluated so it will not interfere [[42:2|AC 91-78A 7.2]], and devices reduce the scan [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15g1(a)]].

final_quiz.q: IFR in IMC, your VOR needle swings each time a passenger's laptop wakes up. Per AC 91.21-1D, what should happen?
options: Nothing; laptops are excepted
Isolate the device, note the conditions, and turn it off
Switch to GPS and keep the laptop on
Ask ATC for a PED waiver
final_quiz.why: If interference from a PED is seen in cruise, isolate the device, record conditions and turn it off [[43:5|AC 91.21-1D 7.2.3]]. Under IFR only devices you determined will not interfere may be used [[60:438|14 CFR 91.21(b)]].

final_quiz.q: Which statement about airborne cell phone use is correct per AC 91.21-1D?
options: The FAA bans all phone use in aircraft, even on the ground
The FCC prohibits airborne cellular operation; the FAA allows phones on the ground
Phones are allowed in flight below 10,000 ft
Only the PIC may use a phone in flight
final_quiz.why: The FCC prohibits airborne cellular telephone operation (47 CFR 22.925), and the FAA allows phones on the ground [[43:7|AC 91.21-1D 9.1]] [[43:7|AC 91.21-1D 9.2]].

final_quiz.q: A passenger needs a medical device that supports breathing. Per AC 91.21-1D:
options: It must be off for taxi, takeoff and landing
It may be used at all times; small ones should be secured on the person for surface movement, takeoff, descent, approach and landing
It needs an FAA waiver
It may be used only above 10,000 ft
final_quiz.why: M-PEDs may be used at all times and need not be switched off; small ones should be secured during surface movement, takeoff, descent, approach and landing [[43:9|AC 91.21-1D 11]].

final_quiz.q: A family wants to scatter a loved one's ashes over a remote ridge. Under 91.15, which is true?
options: It is banned in all cases
It is allowed if it creates no hazard to persons or property, with reasonable precautions
It requires an FAA waiver
Only the passenger is responsible, not the PIC
final_quiz.why: 91.15 bars hazardous drops but does not prohibit dropping with reasonable precautions to avoid injury or damage; the duty is the PIC's [[60:437|14 CFR 91.15]].

final_quiz.q: In cruise on a private VFR flight, an angry passenger threatens you and grabs your arm after you refuse to fly low over his house. Which statement matches the rule text?
options: 91.11 does not apply, since it protects only air carrier crews
91.11 applies: no person may assault, threaten, intimidate or interfere with a crewmember in the performance of duties aboard an aircraft being operated
Only 91.15 applies, because the passenger is creating a hazard
No Part 91 rule applies until the airplane lands
final_quiz.why: 91.11 says "no person" and has no air carrier limit [[60:436|14 CFR 91.11]]. In cruise you are in flight time, so you are a crewmember: a person assigned to perform duty in an aircraft during flight time [[60:4|14 CFR 1.1]] [[60:7|14 CFR 1.1]]. 91.15 is about dropping objects [[60:437|14 CFR 91.15]].

final_quiz.q: You fly a Part 135 charter at 8,000 ft, descending for the approach. A passenger asks you to point out a famous landmark on the PA. What does 135.100 say?
options: Fine, you are below 10,000 ft but in cruise
Not allowed: you are in a critical phase, and pointing out sights is not required for safe operation
Fine if the autopilot is on
Not allowed only during taxi
final_quiz.why: Critical phases include all flight below 10,000 ft except cruise, and announcements pointing out sights of interest are not required for safe operation [[6:33|14 CFR 135.100]].

final_quiz.q: Per AC 91-73B, for an aircraft with no door between the pilots and the passengers, when should passengers keep a sterile cockpit on arrival?
options: From the first radio call to approach until touchdown
From when landing preparations begin until the aircraft is safely stopped at the terminal
Only on short final
From 10,000 ft until the runway turnoff
final_quiz.why: On arrival: from when landing preparations begin until the aircraft is safely stopped at the terminal [[7:5|AC 91-73B 7c]].

final_quiz.q: Why does the AFH say seat and body security matter even when the cabin stays intact in a crash?
options: Belts reduce the aircraft's groundspeed
A loose occupant does not slow with the cabin and is stopped violently in a secondary collision
Belts keep the cabin from collapsing
Belts prevent fire
final_quiz.why: Unless the occupant decelerates at the same rate as the structure, its intactness gives no benefit; the occupant hits the interior in a secondary collision [[24:351|AFH 18-2]].

final_quiz.q: Which passenger briefing items does 91.519 require that 91.107 does not, and does 91.519 apply to your Cessna 182?
options: Doors, exits and survival equipment; no, 91.519 is in subpart F for large and turbojet-powered multiengine airplanes
Belts only; yes
Smoking only; yes, for all airplanes
Oxygen only; no, it is for helicopters
final_quiz.why: 91.519 adds smoking, doors and exits, survival equipment, ditching and oxygen [[60:534|14 CFR 91.519]]. Subpart F governs large airplanes, turbojet-powered multiengine airplanes and fractional aircraft [[60:527|14 CFR 91.501]].

takeaways: Before takeoff, brief everyone how to fasten and unfasten belts and harnesses; before taxi, takeoff and landing, tell them to fasten.
Passengers wear belts and installed harnesses for taxi, takeoff and landing. Crew harness: takeoff and landing.
Lap child only under 2 and with no restraining device; child seats need the right labels and a forward-facing seat.
No interfering with a crewmember, no careless or reckless operation, no hazardous drops.
91.21 limits devices on certificate holders' aircraft and under IFR, where you decide what is safe.
Part 91 has no sterile cockpit rule, but brief one: quiet for taxi, departure, arrival and landing.
A tight belt is what lets an occupant use the protection the cabin gives.
cfi_notes: The PHAK SAFETY list says shoulder harness for takeoff and landing [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]], but 91.107(a)(3) requires an installed harness during surface movement too [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)]]. Teach the CFR and point out the narrower handbook line.

Interesting split: required flight crewmembers need the harness only for takeoff and landing [[60:441|14 CFR 91.105]], and 91.107(a)(3) does not apply to them [[60:442|14 CFR 91.107(b)]]. Passengers need it for taxi as well [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)]].

The sources disagree on the sterile window. PHAK: departure to first intermediate altitude and clear of local airspace [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]]. AC 91-73B: from preflight preparations to cruise [[7:5|AC 91-73B 7c]]. 135.100: below 10,000 ft except cruise [[6:33|14 CFR 135.100]]. None is a Part 91 rule; pick one and brief it.

Many pilots think the FAA bans phones in all flight. 91.21 covers certificate holders and IFR only [[60:438|14 CFR 91.21(a)]]; the airborne cellular ban is an FCC rule described in AC 91.21-1D [[43:7|AC 91.21-1D 9.1]].
AC 61-98E App E lists 91.105, 91.107, 91.13, 91.15 and 91.17 [[15:40|AC 61-98E App E]]. Ask the pilot to give a real briefing at the airplane as part of the flight review.
Intoxicated passengers (91.17(b)) are on the AC 61-98E list but are taught in RF.I.E, not here.
For airline pilots: 121.542 is the sterile flight deck rule they know [[25:179|AIH 9-9]], but its text is not in our sources. Use 135.100, which has the same structure [[6:33|14 CFR 135.100]].
Doors-off photo flights are a newer area: 91.108 adds briefing and demonstration duties [[60:445|14 CFR 91.108(g)-(h)]]. Check that the pilot has read it before flying one.
Use the FRAT item to show how the FAA scores a skipped briefing [[30:28|RMH 3-10]], and the AFH 9G numbers to show why belts matter [[24:352|AFH 18-3]].
gaps: The text of 14 CFR 121.542 and 47 CFR 22.925 is not in the sources; only descriptions in the AIH, IPH and AC 91.21-1D are.
No source defines "careless," "reckless" or "reasonable precautions" for 91.13 and 91.15. FAA and NTSB case decisions are not in the sources.
Exit, door, extinguisher and emergency procedures differ by airplane; the POH/AFM, not these sources, gives them.
InFO 13010, 13010SUP and RTCA DO-307A and DO-363, which AC 91.21-1D cites for PED tolerance, are not in the sources.
Child seat makers' labels and weight limits, and FMVSS 213, are not in the sources; check the seat itself.

activities.title: Which rule?
activities.intro: Tap a section, then what it covers.

pairs.r: No dropping objects that create a hazard
Supplemental restraints, doors open or off
Oral briefing in large and turbojet airplanes

activities.title: True or false: devices and stations
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: Portable voice recorders need a PIC determination before use under IFR.
cards.why: False. Portable voice recorders are excepted outright in 91.21(b)(1) [[60:438|14 CFR 91.21(b)]].

cards.s: AC 91.21-1D says an operator whose aircraft has not been shown PED tolerant may allow PED use during cruise.
In AC 91.21-1D, "operator" can mean the PIC or a renter-pilot.
cards.why: True. It means PIC, renter-pilot or air carrier certificate holder [[43:2|AC 91.21-1D 6.1]].

cards.s: 91.21 was first written to stop FM radio receivers from interfering with aircraft systems.
cards.why: True. It was established in 1961 to prohibit FM receivers [[43:1|AC 91.21-1D 6.1]] [[43:2|AC 91.21-1D 6.1]].

cards.s: A required flight crewmember must keep the safety belt fastened while at the station en route.
A required flight crewmember may leave the station en route only in an emergency.
cards.why: False. They may also leave for duties connected with the operation or for physiological needs [[60:441|14 CFR 91.105]].

activities.title: Rule or guidance?
activities.intro: For a Part 91 flight in a piston single, tap each item, then tap where it belongs.
buckets: FAA guidance, not a Part 91 rule here

items.t: Brief each person how to unfasten the belt
Tell everyone to fasten belts before taxi
Each person in an approved seat with belt for landing
Required crew stays at station en route except for duties or needs
Ask for a sterile flight deck during climb out
Show where the fire extinguisher is
Teach passengers how to activate the ELT
Have the right-seat passenger scan for traffic

activities.title: What should passengers do now?
activities.intro: Drag each passenger instruction to the phase of flight where it belongs.

pins.label: Quiet until clear of local airspace
Questions and sights are fine now

activities.title: Work the numbers
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: AFH: at a uniform 9G, stopping from 50 mph takes about 9.4 ft. Stopping distance grows with the square of groundspeed. About how many feet to stop from 75 mph?
Doubling groundspeed quadruples destructive energy (energy goes with speed squared). Touching down at 60 mph groundspeed instead of 45 mph gives how many times the energy?
Touchdown airspeed 55 knots. Landing into a 15-knot headwind versus with a 15-knot tailwind: how many times more energy with the tailwind?
items.why: Groundspeeds: 55 - 15 = 40 and 55 + 15 = 70 knots. (70 / 40)^2 = 1.75^2 = 3.06. Groundspeed governs crash severity [[24:352|AFH 18-3]].

items.q: Score the RMH sample FRAT: did not sleep well (2), feel a bit off (2), destination 6 SM and 4,000 ft ceilings (1), great day (0), night (3), no hurry (1), used charts and computer to assist (0), did not use a computer program for all planning (0), weight and balance verified (0), performance evaluated (0), passengers not briefed (2). Total?
items.why: 2 + 2 + 1 + 0 + 3 + 1 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 2 = 11, in the 10 to 20 "exercise caution" band. Briefing the passengers (0 instead of 2) drops it to 9, in the 0 to 10 "not complex flight" band [[30:28|RMH 3-10]].

items.q: Application: light airplanes are designed for 9G forward crash loads. What forward load, in pounds, would a 170 lb occupant put into the belt and harness at 9G?
items.why: 9 x 170 = 1,530 lb. The 9G design figure is from the AFH [[24:352|AFH 18-3]]; the multiplication is our application.

activities.title: Passengers from ramp to ramp
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put these in order, then tap Check.
steps: Check belts, harnesses and seat locks on the preflight
Brief how to fasten and unfasten belts, plus the SAFETY items
Tell everyone to fasten belts and harnesses before taxi
Quiet cabin from taxi until clear of the local airspace
Cruise: talk, point out sights, keep passengers informed
Quiet cabin again from the start of descent until parked
Shut down, deplane passengers, then the post-flight inspection
activities.why: Preflight [[24:41|AFH 2-4]]; briefing [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(1)]] [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]]; notify [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(2)]]; sterile periods [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]] [[7:5|AC 91-73B 7c]]; low workload [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]]; deplaning before the post-flight walk around [[24:60|AFH 2-23]].

activities.title: Can I do this flight? A family hop
activities.intro: You are flying a Cessna 172 on a Saturday with your friend Dan, his wife Maria and their 18-month-old son. It is a VFR sightseeing flight from your home field.

steps.s: At the airplane, Maria plans to hold the baby in a front-pack carrier buckled to her chest. What do you do?
options: Allow it; the carrier adds protection
Allow it only if her belt also goes around the carrier
Have her hold him without the carrier, or use an approved, labeled child seat in its own seat
Leave the baby at the FBO
steps.why: A lap child under 2 must not use any restraining device [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)(i)]]. An approved child seat needs the right labels on a forward-facing seat [[60:442|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)(iii)]].

steps.s: Dan says he has flown a lot and does not need the briefing. What is the minimum you must still cover with him?
options: Nothing, since he is experienced
How to fasten and unfasten his belt and harness, and a notice to fasten before taxi, takeoff and landing
Only the location of the fire extinguisher
Only the sterile cockpit rule
steps.why: Each person on board must be briefed and notified [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(1)]] [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(2)]].

steps.s: During taxi, Dan starts a phone call to film the takeoff live for his family. What do you say?
options: Fine, phones are allowed on the ground
End the call; phones off or in airplane mode for taxi and takeoff, and quiet until we are clear of the local airspace
Fine, but keep the volume low
Only if he uses a headset
steps.why: Devices are discouraged during taxi and everyone should turn them off then [[7:5|AC 91-73B 7b(j)]]. A call carried into the takeoff would also be airborne cellular use, which the FCC prohibits [[43:7|AC 91.21-1D 9.1]]. Ask for a sterile cabin through departure [[7:5|AC 91-73B 7c]] [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]].

steps.s: Right after liftoff, Dan's door pops open with a loud bang. He reaches for it and starts to unbuckle. What now?
options: Help him close it while climbing
Tell him to stay belted and leave the door; fly the airplane, fly a normal pattern and land
Land immediately on the remaining runway at any cost
Slip hard toward the door to slam it
steps.why: Concentrate on flying, do not rush to land, fly a normal pattern, and do not release the belt to reach the door [[24:366|AFH 18-17]].

steps.s: Later Dan asks to drop a bag of flower petals over a friend's crowded beach party. What applies?
options: Any drop is illegal
Drops are fine anywhere if the bag is small
You may not allow a drop that creates a hazard; with a crowd below, reasonable precautions are hard to show, so say no
Drops are fine if ATC approves
steps.why: No PIC may allow a hazardous drop; dropping is allowed only with reasonable precautions to avoid injury or damage [[60:437|14 CFR 91.15]]. A low, close pass over a crowd also raises 91.13 [[60:436|14 CFR 91.13]].
